scenes.say: Two lines add a point to a vector. One builds it twice, the other once. By the end, you'll write the erase remove idiom from memory, and pick the right container and sort for any task.

Interviewers ask these seven questions again and again. Today you count constructor calls, and tell reserve from resize. Then you choose a container and a sort, see a heap inside a vector, and delete the right way.
lines: Pick a container, a comparator, a sort

scenes.title: Who builds the point?
scenes.statement: Add the point one, two to a vector two ways. Count the constructor and move calls in each way.
scenes.say: Two lines add a point to a vector. For example, push back of a finished point, and emplace back of two numbers. Count the calls.

scenes.head: Cooking at the table
scenes.say: Think of a restaurant. Push back cooks the dish in the kitchen, carries it over, and throws the pan away. Emplace back cooks it right at the table. Same dish, fewer steps.

scenes.head: Count the constructor calls
scenes.say: The struct prints which constructor runs. Push back takes a finished object. So P of one, two is built, then moved in. Emplace back takes the arguments, and builds the element in place. We reserve first, so growth adds no extra moves.
Your turn. We already hold a string s, and write emplace back of s. Copy, move, or something cleverer? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Emplace is not magic
scenes.say: A copy. Emplace back of an existing object still copies it, same as push back. It wins with a literal: push back builds a temporary string first. The trap: emplace back can call explicit constructors. Push back of a raw new won't compile. Emplace back does, and can leak.

scenes.head: reserve is not resize
scenes.say: Now a second mix-up. Reserve four only allocates: size stays zero. Resize four creates four zeros: size four. Push back seven onto each. The reserved vector gets one element. The resized one gets five. That is the classic bug.

scenes.head: reserve versus resize
scenes.say: Reserve only allocates. Resize changes the size, and creates zeros. Index after reserve? Undefined, no element exists. Resize can shrink size, not capacity. Reserve before push back loops. Resize to index.

scenes.title: Which sequence container?
scenes.statement: Three containers hold a sequence. Choose by memory layout: random access, fast front, cheap middle inserts.
scenes.say: Vector, deque, or list? For example, a job queue, and a list you splice. Which layout fits? Mostly, vector.

scenes.head: Shelf, rows, treasure hunt
scenes.say: Think of a bookshelf, a set of shelf rows, and a treasure hunt. A vector is one long shelf. A deque is short rows plus an index card. A list is a treasure hunt: every clue points to the next.

scenes.head: The numbers behind the layout
scenes.say: Random access: vector and deque are one step. List must walk. Front inserts: vector shifts everything, the other two don't. Middle inserts: only list, if you hold an iterator. Memory: list pays two pointers per element. Cache: vector wins by far.
Your turn. A queue: push at the back, pop at the front, a million times. Which container is the usual choice? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Queue: push back, pop front, a million times. Best?

scenes.head: Pick by access pattern
scenes.say: Deque. It's fast at both ends, and it's the default behind queue and stack. Vector stays the default for everything else: it's cache friendly. List earns its place with stable iterators, and splice, which moves nodes without copying one element.

scenes.title: Sort by my own rule
scenes.statement: Sort students by grade, highest first. Ann and Cid both scored ninety. Which one comes first?
scenes.say: Four students need ranking. For example, Ann and Cid tie at ninety. Bob and Dan tie at eighty five. Who comes first in a tie?

scenes.head: A comparator answers one question
scenes.say: A comparator answers: should a come before b? Plain sort uses less than: ascending. Pass a lambda returning a greater than b, and it's descending. The library also ships greater. Any callable that takes two elements and returns bool works.

scenes.head: In a set, it defines equal
scenes.say: For a set, the comparator is part of the type. This one orders strings by length. Kiwi, fig, pear go in. What prints? Pause and predict.
How many words does the set print, and which? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `set<string, ByLength>` from kiwi, fig, pear: what prints?

scenes.head: Equivalent means not unique
scenes.say: Fig and kiwi. Where did pear go? A set treats two keys as the same when neither comes first. Kiwi and pear both have length four, so neither is smaller. Pear counts as a duplicate, and is dropped. Your comparator also defines what equal means.

scenes.head: The one rule: strict
scenes.say: The rule: a comparator must be a strict weak ordering. Comparing an element with itself must give false. Less than or equal breaks that, and with sort it's undefined behavior, even a crash. Use strict less than. For several keys, compare tuples with tie.

scenes.head: Stable keeps the tie order
scenes.say: Back to the students. A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order. Ann was before Cid, so Ann stays before Cid. Bob was before Dan, so Bob stays before Dan. Plain sort promises only the grades. A tie may come out either way.

scenes.head: sort versus stable_sort
scenes.say: Equal elements: sort may reorder them, stable sort keeps them. Algorithms: introsort against merge sort. Cost: both O of n log n. Stable needs a buffer. Sort is usually faster. Use stable sort for passes by several keys.
rows: O(n log n) with a buffer (else n log² n)

scenes.title: Always the biggest, fast
scenes.statement: Push five, one, eight, three into a priority queue. Top must return the biggest in constant time. How is it stored?
scenes.say: How does top return the biggest instantly? For example, push five, one, eight, three. How does it store them?

scenes.head: A heap: every parent is the biggest
scenes.say: Think of a company chart where every boss earns at least as much as their reports. Push five: it is the boss. Push one: a report. Push eight: it lands at the bottom, beats its boss, so they swap. Push three: it beats the one, so they swap. Eight sits on top.

scenes.head: The tree is just an array
scenes.say: No pointers. The tree lives in a vector: eight, three, five, one. Top is index zero. Children of index i sit at two i plus one and two i plus two. Pop moves the last element to the root, and sifts it down.

scenes.head: Pop them all
scenes.say: Push the four, then pop until empty. Push sifts up, pop sifts down, each O of log n. Out come eight, five, three, one: always the biggest left. Default is a max heap.
Your turn. Same four numbers, but the queue is declared with greater. What does top return? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: Min-heap, and the comparator twist
scenes.say: One. Greater makes a min heap, and you must spell the container too. A custom comparator reads backwards: it returns true when a has lower priority than b. Build from a range is O of n. You can't iterate it, search it, or change a priority.

scenes.title: Delete every two
scenes.statement: Remove every two from one, two, three, two, four. Do it in one pass, without shifting the tail again and again.
scenes.say: Deleting from a vector, the right way. For example, one, two, three, two, four. Remove the twos. Result: one, three, four.

scenes.head: remove shifts, erase cuts
scenes.say: Take one, two, three, two, four. Remove the twos. Here's the surprise: remove doesn't erase anything. It shifts the keepers forward: three into slot one, four into slot two. It returns the new logical end. Past it are leftovers, and size is still five. Then erase cuts them, and size is three.

scenes.head: The idiom, and the modern way
scenes.say: Put together, it is one line: erase of remove, to the end. Remove if takes a condition. It's one pass, O of n. Erasing matches one by one would be O of n squared. In C plus plus twenty, just call erase or erase if.
Your turn. We forget the second argument: erase of remove, with only one argument, on one, two, three, two, four. How many elements remain? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: The classic trap
scenes.say: Four. With one argument, erase cuts just a single leftover element, so the leftovers stay. And if nothing matched, remove returns end, and erasing end is undefined. Always pass v dot end. For a list, use its own remove member: it unlinks nodes, no shifting.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Push back versus emplace back? Push back takes an object you have. Emplace back takes constructor arguments and builds in place. An existing object still copies.
rows: copies or moves an existing object
existing objects still copy; explicit ctors allowed

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Vector, deque, list? Vector is one contiguous block, fast and cache friendly. Deque is chunks, fast at both ends. List is linked nodes, with cheap splice. Default to vector.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Custom comparator? A function answering: does a come before b? It must be strict: comparing x with itself gives false. Never less than or equal. In a set, it also defines equality.
rows: strict weak ordering: `cmp(x, x)` is false
also defines which keys are equal

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Priority queue? A binary heap in a vector. Top is O of one. Push and pop are O of log n. Max heap by default. Greater gives a min heap.
rows: binary heap stored in a vector
top O(1); push, pop O(log n)

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Sort versus stable sort? Stable sort keeps equal elements in their original order. Both O of n log n, sort is usually faster. Use stable for multi-key passes.
rows: stable keeps the order of equal elements
both O(n log n); stable needs a buffer
cues: Both O of n log n

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Erase remove idiom? Remove only shifts keepers forward and returns the new end. Erase then cuts the leftovers. In C plus plus twenty, call erase or erase if.
rows: shifts keepers forward; returns new end

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Reserve versus resize? Reserve allocates, size stays zero. Resize creates elements, size becomes n. Reserve before push back, resize before indexing.

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode twenty seven, Remove Element, is the erase remove idea. LeetCode two fifteen, Kth Largest Element in an Array, uses a priority queue. LeetCode fifty six, Merge Intervals, sorts with a comparator.
rows: LeetCode 215 · Kth Largest Element in an Array

scenes.say: So say this. Emplace builds in place, reserve only makes room. A comparator must be strict, and stable sort keeps ties. A heap is an array, and erase remove is two steps.
lines: Emplace builds in place; reserve only makes room.
Comparators are strict; stable_sort keeps ties.
A heap is an array. Erase-remove is two steps.
